<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
A comprehensive SEO strategy is being implemented. This covers site titles, schema markup, keyword relevance, and human-personalized AI suggestions.

A centralized SEO configuration file will manage site metadata and keywords. A lightweight custom hook will handle page titles without extra dependencies. Default meta tags will be added to index.html. JSON-LD schemas will include Person, WebSite, ProfessionalService, and ProfilePage markup. A sitemap.xml and updated robots.txt will be generated.

Per-route meta data will be injected via a custom hook. A dedicated schema component will render JSON-LD markup. Google Analytics route tracking will be added to the main App component. A placeholder Open Graph image is being considered since no profile photo exists yet.

An environment example file will hold the production site URL for SEO configuration. Static meta tags in index.html will reference the live domain directly. The placeholder Open Graph image will be created as a simple SVG for conversion to PNG.

The Person schema will include `sameAs` links to professional profiles, `knowsAbout` arrays for specific technologies, and `jobTitle` or `worksFor` fields. AI assistants and search engines increasingly rely on these structured identity signals. The strategy will pair this with `ProfessionalService` markup, clear service descriptions, `areaServed` coverage, and potentially `makesOffer` to signal business availability.</details></think>

_**Agent (default)**_

SEO is in place. Here’s what changed and how it maps to your four goals.

## What was implemented

### 1. Site & page titles
Replaced placeholder `KN20` branding with real titles:

| Route | Title |
|-------|-------|
| `/` | Nazeem Khodabux \| Senior Full-Stack Developer |
| `/start-project` | Start a Project \| Nazeem Khodabux |
| 404 | Page Not Found \| Nazeem Khodabux |

Per-route titles update via `usePageMeta` as users navigate. `index.html` has the homepage defaults for crawlers that don’t run JS.

### 2. Schema markup (JSON-LD)
Added structured data in two places:
- **Static** in `index.html` (Person + WebSite) for basic crawlers
- **Dynamic** via `SeoSchema.tsx` on the homepage with a full graph:

| Schema | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| **Person** | Who you are — name, role, location, skills, social profiles |
| **ProfilePage** | Tells search engines this site is your professional profile |
| **WebSite** | Site identity, linked to you as publisher |
| **ProfessionalService** | What you offer — migrations, commerce, ERP, AI work |
| **ContactPage** | `/start-project` as your inquiry entry point |

### 3. Keyword relevance
Keywords are aligned with your actual work in `src/lib/seo.ts`:
- Meta `keywords` tag
- Meta `description` (mentions Mauritius, e-commerce, ERP, legacy, LLM)
- Schema `knowsAbout` (Vue, Nuxt, React, GraphQL, etc.)
- Schema `serviceType` (legacy migration, headless commerce, etc.)

Target phrases: *full stack developer Mauritius*, *legacy PHP migration*, *headless commerce developer*, *ERP developer*, *LLM integration developer*, etc.

### 4. Person schema for AI discoverability
This is what that earlier AI suggestion was about. **`Person` schema** is how machines build a verified identity graph:

- `sameAs` → GitHub, LinkedIn, Facebook, Instagram (cross-links your profiles)
- `knowsAbout` → skills/topics you’re associated with
- `hasOccupation` → role + skill summary
- `workLocation` → Curepipe, Mauritius

AI assistants (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews) use this plus your LinkedIn, GitHub, and site content to answer questions like *“Who’s a good full-stack developer in Mauritius for legacy migration?”*

`ProfessionalService` schema adds the business angle — what you do and who you serve (Mauritius + worldwide).

---

## New files

- `src/lib/seo.ts` — single source of truth for all SEO data
- `src/hooks/usePageMeta.ts` — updates title, meta, canonical, GA pageviews
- `src/components/SeoSchema.tsx` — injects JSON-LD
- `public/sitemap.xml` — `/` and `/start-project`
- `public/og-image.svg` — social preview image
- `public/favicon.svg` — NK monogram favicon
- `.env.example` — `VITE_SITE_URL` for environment overrides

---

## After deploy — recommended next steps

1. **Google Search Console** — submit `https://nazeemkhodabux.com/sitemap.xml`
2. **Verify email** in `src/lib/seo.ts` — I used `nazeem@nazeemkhodabux.com`; update if different
3. **OG image PNG** — Twitter/Facebook prefer a 1200×630 PNG over SVG. Export `og-image.svg` → `og-image.png` and update the image path in `seo.ts`
4. **Optional: `llms.txt`** — emerging standard (like `robots.txt` for AI crawlers) to tell AI systems who you are and what you offer. Happy to add this if you want.
5. **LinkedIn** — keep headline/skills aligned with `knowsAbout` in the schema (AI cross-references these)

All SEO config lives in one place — edit `src/lib/seo.ts` to update titles, keywords, services, or social links without touching components.

Want me to add `llms.txt`, create the PNG OG image, or set up Search Console verification meta tag next?

Simply showing where key Markdown files can be found is a great first step. Providing some basic structure helps a language model to find where the information it needs can come from.\n\nThe&#96;llms.txt&#96; file is unusual in that it uses Markdown to structure the information rather than a classic structured format such as XML. The reason for this is that we expect many of these files to be read by language models and agents. Having said that, the information in llms.txt follows a specific format and can be read using standard programmatic-based tools.\n\nThe llms.txt file spec is for files located in the root path&#96;/llms.txt&#96; of a website (or, optionally, in a subpath). A file following the spec contains the following sections as markdown, in the specific order:\n\nZero or more markdown sections delimited by H2 headers, containing “file lists” of URLs where further detail is available\n\n- Each “file list” is a markdown list, containing a required markdown hyperlink&#96;[name](url)&#96;, then optionally a&#96;:&#96; and notes about the file.\n\nHere is a mock example:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n# Title\n\n\u003e Optional description goes here\n\nOptional details go here\n\n## Section name\n\n- [Link title](https://link_url): Optional link details\n\n## Optional\n\n- [Link title](https://link_url)\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nNote that the “Optional” section has a special meaning—if it’s included, the URLs provided there can be skipped if a shorter context is needed. Use it for secondary information which can often be skipped.\n\n## Existing standards\n\nllms.txt is designed to coexist with current web standards. While sitemaps list all pages for search engines,&#96;llms.txt&#96; offers a curated overview for LLMs. It can complement robots.txt by providing context for allowed content. The file can also reference structured data markup used on the site, helping LLMs understand how to interpret this information in context.\n\nThe approach of standardising on a path for the file follows the approach of&#96;/robots.txt&#96; and&#96;/sitemap.xml&#96;. robots.txt and&#96;llms.txt&#96; have different purposes—robots.txt is generally used to let automated tools know what access to a site is considered acceptable, such as for search indexing bots. On the other hand,&#96;llms.txt&#96; information will often be used on demand when a user explicitly requests information about a topic, such as when including a coding library’s documentation in a project, or when asking a chat bot with search functionality for information. Our expectation is that&#96;llms.txt&#96; will mainly be useful for inference, i.e. at the time a user is seeking assistance, as opposed to for training. However, perhaps if&#96;llms.txt&#96; usage becomes widespread, future training runs could take advantage of the information in&#96;llms.txt&#96; files too.\n\nsitemap.xml is a list of all the indexable human-readable information available on a site. This isn’t a substitute for&#96;llms.txt&#96; since it:\n\n- Often won’t have the LLM-readable versions of pages listed\n- Doesn’t include URLs to external sites, even though they might be helpful to understand the information\n- Will generally cover documents that in aggregate will be too large to fit in an LLM context window, and will include a lot of information that isn’t necessary to understand the site.\n\n## Example\n\nHere’s an example of&#96;llms.txt&#96;, in this case a cut down version of the file used for the FastHTML project (see also the full version):\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n# FastHTML\n\n\u003e FastHTML is a python library which brings together Starlette, Uvicorn, HTMX, and fastcore's &#96;FT&#96; It follows the [llms.txt spec](https://llmstxt.org/):

```bash

curl https://nazeemkhodabux.com/sitemap.xml
```

Note: `llms.txt` adoption is still early — no major model fetches it automatically yet — but it’s low effort and positions you well as tooling catches up. The Person schema + this file together give AI systems a clear identity + services map.

Wired up **Web3Forms** — free tier is **250 submissions/month**, emails you directly, no backend.

## Setup (one-time, ~2 min)

1. Go to [web3forms.com](https://web3forms.com) and sign up with `khodabux.n@gmail.com`
2. Copy your **Access Key**
3. In **Dokploy** → your app → **Environment Variables**, add:
   ```
   VITE_WEB3FORMS_ACCESS_KEY=your-key-here
   ```
4. **Redeploy** — Vite bakes env vars in at build time, so a rebuild is required

For local dev, create `.env` from `.env.example` with the same key.

## What happens on submit

Form POSTs to Web3Forms → you get an email with all fields (project types, business info, budget, timeline, contact details). The button shows **Sending…** while in flight; errors surface in the footer if something fails.

## Why Web3Forms over alternatives

| Service | Free tier |
|---------|-----------|
| **Web3Forms** | 250/month |
| Formspree | 50/month |
| Getform | 50/month |

For a portfolio with low volume, this is the best free fit — no server, no DB, just email notifications.

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
The `.env` file is missing from `.gitignore`. This could expose sensitive configuration data.

The Dockerfile does not pass the Web3Forms access key as a build argument. Runtime environment variables set by Dokploy will not be available during the Docker build. The Dockerfile needs an `ARG` declaration for `VITE_WEB3FORMS_ACCESS_KEY` followed by an `ENV` assignment before the build step.

Dokploy may not pass build arguments through Dockerfile builds. A better approach is to load the Web3Forms key at runtime from a public `/config.json` file. This avoids build-time environment variable issues entirely.

Runtime loading from a public JSON file would still require manual server-side setup after deployment. Web3Forms keys are public identifiers, so embedding them directly in the frontend is the standard and simpler approach.

A public `config.json` cannot be committed and then ignored, because Dokploy deploys via git push and the file would be missing from the build. Committing the key directly is safe if Web3Forms restricts it to specific domains, since the key is rate-limited per domain anyway.

The user sees the form error without understanding the setup. The simplest immediate fix is to load the Web3Forms key at runtime from a public `config.json` file, falling back to the `VITE_` environment variable. A `public/config.json.example` should be added to document the required configuration.

The user may not have signed up for Web3Forms yet. The error is simply the missing-key guard firing. The plan is to load the key at runtime from `/config.json`, add a `public/config.json.example` template, and update the Dockerfile to accept build arguments for backward compatibility.

The runtime config loader will prioritize the `VITE_` environment variable and fall back to `config.json`. The Dockerfile will declare both `VITE_WEB3FORMS_ACCESS_KEY` and `VITE_SITE_URL` as build arguments. A local `.env` file will be created from the example template, leaving the Web3Forms key empty for the user to populate.

A runtime `config.json` would be gitignored and missing after deployment, so that path is abandoned. The plan is to use Docker build arguments for Dokploy, a local `.env` file for development, and clear instructions. The `.env` file itself will be added to `.gitignore`, since only `.env.example` should be committed.

FormSubmit.co offers a zero-configuration alternative. It requires only an email address in the form action and eliminates the need for API keys entirely.

FormSubmit.co requires email verification on first submission and may redirect unless called via AJAX. Its endpoint is `https://formsubmit.co/ajax/<email>`. The email address is already visible in `seo.ts`, so using FormSubmit would eliminate API keys, environment variables, and Docker build arguments entirely.</details></think>
